rule_en: English questions follow the pattern QUASI: Question word, Auxiliary, Subject, Infinitive. Use do/does for the present simple and did for the past simple. With the verb be, invert the subject and the verb and don't add an auxiliary.
examples_en: What kind of books do you read?
Where did you learn English?
How often does your cousin visit you?
Are your parents from the same town?
tip: Never add do/does/did to questions with be: 'Where are you from?', not 'Where do you are from?'

rule_en: Use the present simple for habits, routines, opinions and permanent situations. Remember -s for he/she/it and don't/doesn't in negatives. Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often) go before the main verb.
examples_en: She usually gets on well with new people.
My best friend never worries about small things.
He doesn't look like his father at all.
What do you do at weekends?
tip: 'What does he do?' asks about a job; 'What is he doing?' asks about now.

rule_en: Use the present continuous (be + verb-ing) for things happening now, around now, or temporary situations. Also use it to describe photos and scenes. State verbs (know, want, like, need, believe) are not normally continuous.
examples_en: I'm looking for a black jacket in a medium size.
In this photo, my friends are standing outside the theatre.
She's staying with her aunt until the flat is ready.
Why are you wearing a coat? It's warm today!
tip: For photos use the continuous: 'In this picture, people are dancing.'

topic: past simple: regular and irregular verbs
rule_en: Use the past simple for finished actions in the past, often with a time expression (last year, in 2020, two days ago). Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs must be learned (go–went, buy–bought, lose–lost). Questions and negatives use did/didn't + base form.
structure: verb-ed / irregular form; did(n't) + base verb
examples_en: We booked the hotel online and paid by card.
I lost my passport on the last day of the holiday.
They didn't enjoy the tour because it rained all day.
Did you take many photos in Istanbul?
tip: Time expressions for the past: yesterday, last week, ago, in 2015, when I was a child.

rule_en: Use the past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) for an action in progress at a moment in the past, often interrupted by a past simple action: I was walking home when it started to rain. Also use it to set the scene in a story.
examples_en: At nine o'clock we were still having breakfast.
She was taking a photo when a bird landed on her head.
The sun was shining and people were sitting in cafes.
What were you doing at midnight?
tip: Long background action → past continuous; short interrupting action → past simple.

rule_en: Time sequencers order events in a story: first, then, after that, later, when, suddenly, finally. Connectors join ideas: because (reason), so (result), but (contrast), although (surprising contrast).
examples_en: First we parked the car, and then we walked to the centre.
Suddenly the dog started to bark.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
Although it was cold, we sat outside.
tip: because = reason, so = result: 'I stayed home because I was ill' / 'I was ill, so I stayed home.'

rule_en: Use be going to + verb for plans and intentions decided before speaking, and for predictions based on present evidence. Negative: be + not + going to. Questions: be + subject + going to.
examples_en: We're going to rent a car at the airport.
I'm not going to check in any luggage — only hand luggage.
Look at the queue! We're going to wait for hours.
What are you going to do after the flight?
tip: Plan made earlier → going to; instant decision → will.

rule_en: Use the present continuous for fixed future arrangements — plans with a time and place, often written in a diary: We're meeting at six. I'm flying to Moscow on Friday. It is very common with verbs of movement (go, come, leave, arrive).
examples_en: I'm seeing the dentist tomorrow morning.
They're getting married in September.
We're leaving at seven, so don't be late.
She's arriving in Dushanbe on Sunday evening.
tip: Arrangement with a fixed time/place → present continuous; general intention → going to.

rule_en: Defining relative clauses say which person or thing we mean. Use who for people, which for things, that for both, and where for places: A chef is a person who cooks in a restaurant. Don't add a second subject pronoun: 'the man who lives here', not 'the man who he lives here'.
examples_en: A dictionary is a book which explains words.
She's the doctor who helped my grandmother.
That's the cafe where we first met.
I like people that say what they think.
tip: Paraphrasing: if you forget a word, describe it — 'It's a thing which you use for...'

rule_en: Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) with just (a very recent action), already (sooner than expected) and yet (in negatives and questions, until now): I've just finished. She's already done it. Have you washed up yet?
structure: have/has (+ just/already) + participle; ... yet (end of negatives/questions)
examples_en: I've just made the beds.
He's already done the shopping.
Have you cleaned the kitchen yet?
We haven't taken the rubbish out yet.
tip: just/already go in the middle; yet goes at the end.

rule_en: Use the present perfect for recent actions and experiences without a specific time. Use the past simple when the time is stated or finished: I've bought a new bag (recent, no time) vs I bought it last Saturday (time given). Conversations often start in the perfect and continue in the past.
structure: perfect: no time; past simple: finished time
examples_en: I've bought a new jacket. — Really? Where did you buy it?
She's spent all her money. She spent most of it on shoes.
Have you ever returned anything to a shop? — Yes, I returned a shirt last month.
We've been to that shopping centre twice.
tip: Start the topic with the perfect, give the details in the past simple.

rule_en: Compounds with some- appear in positive sentences (something, someone, somewhere); any- in negatives and questions (anything, anyone, anywhere); no- makes the sentence negative with a positive verb (nothing, no one, nowhere). Everything/everyone take a singular verb.
examples_en: I bought something special for the weekend.
Did anyone call while I was out?
There's nothing interesting on TV tonight.
Everyone was excited about the trip.
tip: Don't use two negatives: 'I didn't see anything', not 'I didn't see nothing'.

rule_en: Compare with adjective-er / more + adjective + than. Adverbs usually use more: more quickly. Use as...as for equality and not as...as for difference: He's as tall as his father. It's not as cold as yesterday. Irregular: better, worse, further.
examples_en: The metro is faster than the bus.
She speaks English more fluently than me.
Today isn't as hot as yesterday.
My results are worse than last year.
tip: as...as = the same; not as...as = less.

rule_en: Superlatives compare one thing with the whole group: the biggest, the most beautiful. A very common pattern is superlative + ever + present perfect: It's the best film I've ever seen. After superlatives use in with places: the tallest building in the city.
structure: the + -est / the most + adjective (+ I've ever + participle)
examples_en: It's the most honest city in the world, according to the test.
That was the worst meal I've ever eaten.
She's the friendliest person in our office.
This is the most interesting museum I've ever visited.
tip: 'The best film I've ever seen' — ever + present perfect after a superlative.

rule_en: too + adjective = more than is good (too tired); too much + uncountable, too many + countable. Enough goes AFTER adjectives (not warm enough) but BEFORE nouns (enough time, enough vegetables). not...enough = less than is needed.
structure: too + adj; too much/many + noun; adj + enough; enough + noun
examples_en: I eat too much sugar and I don't do enough exercise.
There are too many cars in the city centre.
This soup isn't hot enough.
Do you drink enough water?
tip: Order: 'enough money' but 'good enough'.

rule_en: Use will/won't + base verb for predictions about the future, often with I think, probably, definitely: I think it'll rain. He probably won't come. Will is the same for all persons.
examples_en: I think our team will win tomorrow.
You'll love this book — it's brilliant.
She probably won't agree with us.
Life will be very different in fifty years.
tip: Position: 'probably' after will but before won't: 'will probably go' / 'probably won't go'.

rule_en: Use will for instant decisions (I'll take this one), promises (I'll always help you), offers (I'll carry that) and requests. Use Shall I...? / Shall we...? for offers and suggestions: Shall I open the window? Shall we start?
examples_en: It's cold — I'll close the window.
I'll pay you back on Friday, I promise.

Shall we take a break?
tip: 'Shall' is used mainly with I and we in offers and suggestions.

topic: review of verb forms: present, past and future
rule_en: Choose the tense by meaning: present simple (habits), present continuous (now/arrangements), past simple (finished past), past continuous (in progress in the past), going to (plans/evidence), will (predictions/decisions). Signal words help: usually, now, yesterday, while, tomorrow, next week.
structure: tense according to time and meaning
examples_en: I usually dream in colour, but last night I dreamt in black and white.
She's sleeping now — call back later.
While I was dreaming, my alarm rang.
Scientists think we'll understand dreams better soon.
tip: Find the time word first, then choose the tense.

topic: uses of the infinitive with to
rule_en: Many verbs are followed by to + infinitive: decide, hope, plan, promise, learn, try, forget, want, need, would like, manage, afford. Also use to + infinitive after adjectives (happy to help) and to express purpose (I called to ask about the job).
structure: verb/adjective + to + base verb; purpose: to + base verb
examples_en: I'm trying to save money for a new laptop.
She managed to finish the report on time.
We're happy to answer any questions.
I went to the shop to buy some bread.
tip: 'To' + infinitive after 'in order' also shows purpose: in order to save time.

rule_en: Some verbs are followed by the gerund (verb + -ing): enjoy, mind, finish, avoid, suggest, imagine, practise, keep, give up. The gerund is also used after prepositions and as the subject of a sentence: Smoking is bad for you.
examples_en: I enjoy meeting new people at work.
She's thinking about changing her job.
Would you mind opening the window?
Learning a language takes time and patience.
tip: After a preposition, always use -ing, never the infinitive: 'good at cooking', not 'good at to cook'.

topic: have to, don't have to, must, mustn't
rule_en: Have to / must express obligation (must is often personal, have to is often external rules). Don't have to means it isn't necessary — you have a choice. Mustn't means it's prohibited — don't do it.
structure: have to / must + base verb; don't have to (no obligation); mustn't (prohibition)
examples_en: I have to wear a uniform at work.
You mustn't park here — it's illegal.
You don't have to bring anything; we have everything we need.
I must call my parents tonight — I promised.
tip: don't have to ≠ mustn't: 'don't have to' = optional, 'mustn't' = forbidden.

rule_en: Use should/shouldn't + base verb to give advice or opinions about what is right or wrong: You should see a doctor. You shouldn't work so much. Use I think/don't think you should... to soften advice.
examples_en: You should talk to him about the problem.
I don't think you should trust him.
We should leave early to avoid the traffic.
Should I apologize to her?
tip: 'Should' is weaker than 'must' — it's advice, not an obligation.

rule_en: Use the first conditional for real, possible future situations: if-clause in the present simple, main clause with will/won't + base verb. The order can be reversed: If it rains, we'll stay in. / We'll stay in if it rains.
structure: If + present simple, ... will + base verb
examples_en: If you study hard, you'll pass the exam.
We won't go to the beach if it's cold.
If she calls, I'll tell her about the meeting.
You'll feel better if you get some sleep.
tip: No comma when 'if' is in the middle: 'We'll stay in if it rains.'

rule_en: Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs) replace a noun after a possessive adjective + noun to avoid repetition: This is my book. This book is mine. Don't confuse them with possessive adjectives, which need a noun after them.
structure: possessive pronoun (stands alone, no noun after it)
examples_en: Is this bag yours or hers?
Our house is bigger than theirs.
This isn't my phone — mine is black.
The mistake wasn't mine; it was his.
tip: 'Its' has no pronoun form because things don't usually 'own' in conversation the same way.

rule_en: Use the second conditional for unreal, imaginary or unlikely situations: if-clause in the past simple, main clause with would + base verb. Use 'were' for all persons in formal style: If I were you...
structure: If + past simple, ... would + base verb
examples_en: If I won the lottery, I'd travel the world.
If she had more time, she would learn a new language.
What would you do if you saw a snake?
If I were you, I'd apologize.
tip: Second conditional is imaginary; first conditional is realistic.

questions.explanation: 'Were' with all persons in this fixed expression.

rule_en: Use the present perfect with for + a period of time (for two years, for a long time) and since + a point in time (since 2019, since Monday) to talk about a situation that started in the past and continues now.
examples_en: I've known her for ten years.
We've lived in this city since 2015.
He's worked here since he finished university.
They haven't spoken for a long time.
tip: for = duration, since = starting point.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: I've had this car ___ three years.
Choose the correct word: She's been afraid of dogs ___ she was a child.
Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Present perfect + since + point in time.

questions.explanation: 'A long time' is a duration → for.

rule_en: Compare unfinished time (present perfect: today, this week, so far) with finished time (past simple: yesterday, last week). The same word can take different tenses depending on whether the period is finished: I've seen her twice this week (unfinished) vs I saw her twice last week (finished).
structure: unfinished period → present perfect; finished period → past simple
examples_en: I've had three coffees today.
I had two coffees yesterday.
We haven't been to the cinema this month.
We didn't go to the cinema last month.
tip: Ask: is the time period over or still going? That decides the tense.

questions.explanation: 'So far today' — unfinished period → present perfect.

rule_en: Use verbs of movement with prepositions to describe action: run into, walk across, jump over, climb up, swim through, go past. The preposition shows the direction or path of the movement.
examples_en: The players ran onto the pitch.
She swam across the lake in twenty minutes.
We walked through the old town.
The ball flew over the fence.
tip: Learn verb + preposition pairs together, like vocabulary chunks.

rule_en: Separable phrasal verbs (turn off, pick up, give back) can be split by a noun object, but a pronoun object must go between the verb and particle: Turn off the light. / Turn it off (not Turn off it). Inseparable phrasal verbs (look after, get on) are never split.
structure: verb + noun + particle / verb + particle + noun; verb + pronoun + particle
examples_en: Can you turn off the TV? / Can you turn it off?
She picked up the phone. / She picked it up.
He looks after his little sister.
Please fill in this form.
tip: With pronouns, the particle always comes after: 'switch it on', never 'switch on it'.

rule_en: Form the passive with be + past participle: is made, was built, has been designed. Use it when the action is more important than who did it, or the doer is unknown/obvious: This phone was made in China. By + agent is optional.
structure: subject + be + past participle (+ by + agent)
examples_en: This bridge was built in 1930.
English is spoken in many countries.
The letter hasn't been sent yet.
The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci.
tip: Change tense of 'be' to match the tense you need: is/was/has been + participle.

rule_en: Use used to + base verb for past habits and states that are now finished: I used to play the piano (but I don't now). Negative: didn't use to. Questions: Did you use to...? Don't confuse with 'be used to' (being accustomed to something).
structure: used to / didn't use to / Did ... use to + base verb
examples_en: We used to live in a small village.
She didn't use to like vegetables when she was young.
Did you use to walk to school?
He used to smoke, but he gave up two years ago.
tip: used to has no present form — for present habits, just use the present simple.

questions.explanation: After 'didn't' the base form is 'use to' (no -d).

rule_en: Use might + base verb for possibility, especially about the future — less certain than will: I might go to the party, I'm not sure yet. Negative: might not (no contraction). Might is the same for all persons and never takes -s or 'to'.
examples_en: I might visit my parents this weekend.
She might not come — she's very busy.
We might travel to Bukhara next year.
It might rain later, so take an umbrella.
tip: might = maybe + will; it shows you're not sure.

rule_en: Use so + auxiliary + subject to agree with a positive statement: I like tea. — So do I. Use neither/nor + auxiliary + subject to agree with a negative statement: I don't like coffee. — Neither do I. The auxiliary must match the original verb tense.
structure: So + aux + subject (agree positive); Neither/Nor + aux + subject (agree negative)
examples_en: I love travelling. — So do I.
She's from Tashkent. — So is my friend.
I haven't been to Japan. — Neither have I.
He can't swim. — Neither can she.
tip: Match the auxiliary to the tense: is→so is, do→so do, can→so can, have→so have.

rule_en: Use the past perfect (had + past participle) for an action that happened before another past action: When I arrived, the train had already left. It shows the earlier of two past events.
examples_en: By the time we got to the cinema, the film had started.
She had never seen snow before she moved to Russia.
I realized I had forgotten my keys.
They had already eaten when we arrived.
tip: Two past events: the EARLIER one gets 'had + participle'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: When we arrived, the meeting ___.
Choose the correct form: She ___ never ___ sushi before that trip.
questions.explanation: Before a past reference point → past perfect.

By 2020, they have lived there for ten years.

questions.explanation: Past perfect for duration before a past point.

rule_en: When we report what someone said, tenses usually move one step back: present simple→past simple, present continuous→past continuous, present perfect→past perfect, will→would, can→could. Pronouns and time expressions also change: 'I' → 'he/she', 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'.
examples_en: 'I'm tired,' she said. → She said she was tired.
'I'll call you,' he said. → He said he would call me.
'I've finished,' they said. → They said they had finished.
'I can help,' she said. → She said she could help.
tip: 'Say' doesn't need an object (say something); 'tell' needs a person (tell someone something).

rule_en: When the question word (who, what, which) is the SUBJECT of the sentence, don't use do/does/did — keep normal word order: Who called you? (not Who did call you?) Compare with object questions, which need the auxiliary: Who did you call?
structure: Subject question: QW + verb (no auxiliary); Object question: QW + auxiliary + subject + verb
examples_en: Who broke the window?
What happened at the meeting?
Which team won the match?
Who did you meet at the party?
tip: Ask: is the question word the subject (doing the action) or the object (receiving it)? Subject → no auxiliary.
